changes: Rules 01 and 05 are reworded so each covers only what it was written for. In version 2, rule 01 was read as covering a statement of patent status, which rule 03 covers, and rule 05 was read as covering security claims, which rule 02 covers. The other thirteen rules keep their version 2 text. Records sealed under versions 1 and 2 name their hashes, and rules/v1.json and rules/v2.json are kept so a reader can recompute them.
note: General writing rules for a claims review demo. They are not legal advice and not a compliance standard.

rules.text: Don't say a product is certified, compliant or approved without naming who said so. A statement of patent status is not a claim of certification, compliance or approval.
Don't call anything unbreakable, tamper-proof or 100% secure.
Don't say "patented" unless a patent has actually issued.

A measured figure, such as a speed, a saving, a rate or a count of customers, needs a stated source and date. Prices, trial lengths, ranges that describe who a product is for, version numbers, dates and a percentage used as an absolute claim rather than a measurement are not measured figures.

An absolute claim, using words such as "every", "all", "never" or "no one", needs proof that it holds in every case. A plain statement of what the product does not do or does not need is a stated limit, not an absolute claim. Don't use this rule for a security claim, such as calling something unbreakable, tamper-proof or 100% secure.
Don't promise a legal result, such as "admissible in court" or "protects you from liability." A statement of the company's own patent status is not a promised legal result.
Say plainly what the product doesn't do, next to what it does.
Don't name a customer or partner without permission.
Don't describe a planned feature as if it exists today. Label it as planned.
Don't use "guaranteed" unless a written guarantee exists.
Don't claim to be "the first", "the only" or "the leading" without proof.
Don't compare against a named competitor without a current, checkable source. A claim of rank with no competitor named, such as "the leading", is not a comparison under this rule.
Don't quote a person or company without their approval and the exact wording.
Don't state a result as typical if it came from one test or one customer.
Don't imply that a regulator, government or standards body endorses the product unless it has said so in writing.
